chapter_theme: In the last ilampakam Civakan comes to the assembly of the Jina, with its festival, tree and gods' whisks, bows and circles, hears that a king's renunciation is the excellent course, and the hymns to the Jina's feet place the freedom from deeds in worship and the Jina's word.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who comes to the Jina's assembly
the Jina, the lord of the three umbrellas and the pindi tree, who has shed his deeds
the gods who hold whisks and rain flowers at the Jina's assembly
the unnamed singer who hymns the Jina in the second person (3017-3021), taken as a worshipper in the host or the king

2999.reading: The lutes and flutes sound softly, the drums answer in a guest's welcome, and the bright gem-set instruments are said to pour out their sound as the festival begins.
2999.nuance: The last line reports the sound as hearsay (என்பவே), a poet's formula for scenes he did not see.

3000.reading: Aloe smoke, wish-tree garlands and heaped flowers make earth and sky look like a red-gemmed casket.

3001.reading: Many praise, sing and dance at the city of the lord of the three umbrellas, and the massed instruments sound like a flood of the world roaring.
3001.nuance: The 'lord of the three umbrellas' (முக்குடைச் செல்வன்) is the Jina, whose city is the assembly Civakan is approaching.

3002.reading: Groves, lotus tanks, bee-filled gardens, tall golden walls and white banners are said to spread as if they had joined the sky.

3003.reading: The raised pinnacles, the trident-topped gate-towers and the golden hill-like heights look as if time had brought all the earth together for the eye to see.
3003.nuance: Line 4 (காலமுற்றுடன் கண்ணுற்ற போன்றவே) is hard to parse; the comparison is read loosely.

3004.reading: Gate arches hung with wish-tree garlands, spread over the walls, are said to outshine Indra's golden city while aloe smoke veils the sun.

3005.reading: White birds on the lotus tops look like a white lotus of glory opening in a red lotus, and the poet adds that one could doubt whether they were real.
3005.nuance: Line 3 (ஐயஞ்செய்தடுபா னிறப்புள்ளின) is hard to parse, so the poet's doubt is only partly clear.

3006.reading: The moat like a great sea and the temple with its roaring birds are so fine that, the verse says, heaven would be sweet only if this did not exist on earth.
3006.nuance: The construction of line 3-4 (இல்லை யேற்றுறக்கம் இனிதென்பவே) can be read two ways, as a boast that heaven is lesser or as 'heaven would be sweet if there were no such place'.

3007.reading: A radiant figure comes down from the sky, worships and draws near, and the lord appears like a young sun over the milk-sea on a gem mountain.
3007.nuance: It is not clear whether the one who descends is Civakan, a god, or the one who appears; line 4 names the lord (இறைவன்) as the one who shows himself, and I read him as the Jina.
3007.event: A radiant figure descends, worships and approaches, and the lord appears.

3008.reading: The one who has shed his deeds sits with his hand placed, his face like the sun and the lotus opened at its rising.
3008.nuance: வினையுதிர்த்தவர் (those who shed deeds) is the verse's own name for the liberated, a Jain sense that the narrator holds rather than argues.

claims.claim: the one who has shed his deeds has a form like this, radiant as the sun and the opened lotus

3009.reading: At the sight the king's hair stands up, tears pour, and with love he praises, scatters flowers like rain and circles to the right.
3009.nuance: Line 1 (இரிந்தன விருவினை) may mean the deeds flee at his seeing or that his hairs stand; the claim is taken as the first.
3009.event: Civakan praises with tears, scatters flowers and walks round the Jina keeping him on his right.

claims.claim: at the sight of the liberated one the two kinds of deed scatter

3010.reading: Pearl garlands, gem clusters, golden and coral wreaths and flower strings hang down in profusion.

3011.reading: The gods hold up whisks as if the sea waves had met a gem mountain, and the sweet rays of the three umbrellas drink the dark.
3011.nuance: The whisks and the three umbrellas are the marks of the Jina's assembly; the verse does not say so in words, and the sense is from the scene.
3011.event: The gods fan the Jina with whisks under the three umbrellas.

3012.reading: The Jina's pindi tree opens its flowers, bees gather, and the cuckoo calls as if keeping a festival.
3012.nuance: வீரன் பிண்டியே names the tree as the hero's, the ashoka that marks the Jina.

3013.reading: In the pindi's thick shade, to end the disease of birth, the hero appears and drums announce that all should eat the nectar of dharma.
3013.nuance: Line 2 has a misprint (றோன்னினா for தோன்றினான்); the sense is that he appeared.
3013.event: The Jina appears under the pindi tree and the drums call all to eat the nectar of dharma.

claims.claim: the Jina's presence under the tree ends the disease of birth, and his dharma is a nectar to be eaten

3014.reading: The gods rain flowers and the king reaches the faultless lord whose red feet sit on a honeyed lotus, the one who ends the births of ascetics.
3014.event: Civakan reaches the Jina's feet while the gods rain flowers.

claims.claim: the supreme lord ends the births of ascetics

3015.reading: The one who bows touches his gem crown to the ground and praises, saying that the scion of Civakan's line and the Kasyapa lord may live, while jewelled lutes ring out.
3015.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to parse: the names சீவக குமரன் and காசிப அடிகள் stand in a run of titles and it is not clear whether the praise is of the Jina or the king's own line, and the word மருகலில் is unclear.
3015.event: Civakan bows with his crown to the ground and praises the Kasyapa lord.

3016.reading: The lord's sweet word, that a king's renunciation is the excellent thing, falls like a rain-cloud's thunder out of his mouth, like gold hill opened.
3016.nuance: The word of the Jina is given as a narrated report in the poet's words, not in direct speech, and the sense of the second line (the hill opening its mouth) is a simile for the voice.
3016.event: The Jina tells Civakan that the king's renunciation is the excellent course.

claims.claim: for a king, to renounce is the excellent thing

3017.reading: Speaking to the lord of the knowers, the singer says he was born in the unsafe course like a morsel between an elephant's tusks and feared his deeds, and that those who circle the lotus-treading feet seem not to suffer.
3017.nuance: The speaker is not named; the 'I' who feared is read as Civakan or as a worshipper in the host. Lines 3-4 are hard to parse. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

claims.claim: beings are born in the dangerous course through evil deeds and fear their fruit
those who circle the Jina's feet do not suffer

3018.reading: In praise to the lord whose garland never fades under the pindi, the singer says that the world does not sing of those who do not sing his virtues and that those who do not wear the flowers of his feet are not worn by the gods.
3018.nuance: The second half of the stanza is hard to parse (பாடாதாரைப் பாடாது உலகம், சூடார்மலை ...), so the claim is a loose reading. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

claims.claim: those who do not praise the Jina's virtues are not praised in return

3019.reading: The singer says that those who do not reach the lord on his gem seat, praised by all three worlds, are kicked by their fierce deeds, fall into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread in a weaver's spool.
3019.nuance: The comparison in line 4 is of a thread wound on the shuttle (நெய்யும் நுண்ணூல் நாழிகையில் நிரம்பா நின்று): the same thread goes round without end. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

claims.claim: those who do not come to the Jina fall under their deeds and whirl in a sea of sorrow

3020.reading: The singer addresses the lord, calm as a moon among stars, who sat as the ancient master and spoke while beings wept under their deeds, and says that those who say his word will not suffer for countless years.
3020.nuance: Line 2 (முதுவாய் வலவையாயிருந்து) is hard to parse; வலவை reads as a skilled speaker. Line 4's first half is repeated at the start of 3021's last line, which suggests a refrain or a copyist's slip. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

claims.claim: those who repeat the Jina's word are freed of suffering for ages

3021.reading: The singer says he sank in the sea of birth, came to the lord's feet on a golden throne of gems, and asks whether it would be fair to go again.
3021.nuance: The word னருவாய் in line 4 is corrupt and the question's sense cannot be fixed. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

claims.claim: the one who has come to the Jina's feet has risen out of the sea of birth

3022.reading: The king bows with his gem crown, with his ear-rings, gold bands, garland of pearls and flower cluster shining on the ground, to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees.
3022.nuance: The lotus under the walking feet is the Jina's own seat among the lotuses in the assembly; the verse names no person, and the 'king' is taken from the crown.
3022.event: Civakan bows with his crown to the Jina's feet.

3023.reading: The lord of the jewel crown bows, while the sky wonders, to the sea of countless virtues, the wheel of dharma that guards life and clears the world's darkness of hunger, hatred and disease, and whose limit is wisdom.
3023.nuance: The verse names both அறவாழி (wheel of dharma) and குணக்கடல் (sea of virtues): the same Tamil element ஆழி/கடல் is both a wheel and a sea here.
3023.event: Civakan bows to the Jina with the gods wondering.

claims.claim: the Jina's wheel of dharma guards life and clears the world's darkness of hunger, hatred and disease

links.note: 2555 has the city say that anyone who sees how Civakan was born in the burning ground, grew up a merchant's son and was worshipped by kings must ask why live heedless instead of doing penance; 3016 has the Jina tell the king that renunciation is the excellent thing.
links.teaches: The people's question about heedlessness at the crowning is answered by the lord's own word here, so the end of the book fulfils what its hero's rise had begun to pose.

links.note: 2560 has Civakan circle the shrine and say he has been born and will not be born again; 3017 has a worshipper at the end say he was born in a fearful course and feared his deeds, and that those who circle the feet do not suffer.
links.teaches: The coronation-day boast of no more births is brought to its ground at the end, where the fear of deeds, not the pride of a king, is what sends the worshipper to the feet.

links.note: 2563 hymns the lord as the one who understood without fault, the wheel that removes stain, and who set bounds to the senses; 3023 hymns the same lord as the sea of virtues and the wheel of dharma that clears hunger, hatred and disease.
links.teaches: The same epithets, wheel and a sea of virtues, recur at the king's last bow, so the earlier hymn's titles are seen to be the book's one settled form of praise.

links.note: Kural 342 says renounce while there is something to renounce, and many things come after; 3016 has the Jina tell a king, who has the most to give up, that renunciation is the excellent course.
links.teaches: The Kural counsels renunciation in general and never says who it is hardest for, and the verse sets it before a crowned king as the hardest case.

gains.a: the Jina's counsel to the king gets a general rule that one can renounce only what one still holds, which is why the king's case is the gravest
gains.b: the Kural's bare 'renounce while it is yours' gets a concrete test, a ruler with a whole kingdom to give up

links.note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births and others cannot; 3019 says those who do not reach the lord are kicked by their deeds into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread on a shuttle.
links.teaches: The Kural states the crossing and the failure to cross but gives no cause or picture for the failure, and the verse supplies deeds that beat the swimmer down and a turning that never ends.

gains.a: the verse's sea of sorrow is given the Kural's single condition for crossing it, reaching the lord's feet
gains.b: the Kural's 'cannot swim' is given a cause (deeds that strike) and a picture (thread wound without end on a shuttle)

links.note: 3020 praises the Jina as the master whose spoken word frees those who repeat it from suffering; Tirumanthiram 105 has the Lord stand beyond the two kinds of deed.
links.teaches: Jain release comes by hearing and keeping the word of one who went before, while the Saiva text puts the Lord beyond deeds so that deeds cannot reach him, and the two disagree on whether a liberated one also helps.

gains.a: the praise of a teacher whose word wears away deeds is shown as a path with no god above it who removes them
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord beyond both deeds meets a rival in which the one beyond deeds is a teacher who shows a way and does not grant grace

links.note: 3022 has the king bow to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees; Kural 3 praises those who reach the feet of the one who walked on the flower.
links.teaches: Both place the object of worship on the lotus, the Kural without a name and the epic with a figure the king can bow to, so the stock image is shown being used as a scene.

gains.a: the verse's lotus-treading feet are shown as the stock image of the Kural's opening praise, so the king's bow is the act the couplet commends
gains.b: the Kural's 'one who walked on the flower' gets a staged scene, a lotus in an assembly with a king bowing before it

links.note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a dead sense; 3022 has the king bow with his gem crown, ear-rings and bands shining on the ground.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the cost of a head that does not bow, and the epic shows the most ornamented head in the book putting its crown to use by bowing.

gains.a: the king's crown, ear-rings and garlands are given their one use, the bow, which the couplet makes the measure of a head
gains.b: the Kural's useless head gets its opposite, a head heavy with ornaments that is not useless because it bows

links.note: Kural 8 says other seas are hard to swim except for those who reach the feet of the one called அறவாழி; 3023 uses அறவாழி for the wheel of dharma and also calls him a sea of virtues.
links.teaches: The Kural's single word அறவாழி can be a sea or a wheel, and the epic shows the lord named as both in one verse.

gains.a: the verse's wheel of dharma and sea of virtues are read as the two sides of one name, so its praise echoes the couplet's term in both senses
gains.b: the Kural's compound அறவாழி gets a use in which it is a wheel and the sea is named separately, so its single word is seen to carry two images

source_issues: Verses 3017-3021 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
3007 and 3015 do not say plainly who descends or who bows.
3013 line 2 has a misprint (றோன்னினா for தோன்றினான்).
3021 line 4 has a corrupt word (னருவாய்) and repeats the first half of 3020 line 4.
